newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Canada calls for conflict cooperation after Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada calls for conflict cooperation after Zaire.

text.p: Canada told a European security summit on Monday that the crisis in Zaire had shown the need for the international community to work out a way of facing up faster to such emergencies so that it can save more lives.

"We need to put into place the mechanisms that in future will allow us to respond to the next Zaire in a faster, better organised manner," Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien told leaders from over 50 nations at the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) summit in Lisbon.
"I propose that the OSCE collaborate with other security institutions to address this problem as a matter of priority," he said in his speech to the opening session.
Chretien said the Zaire crisis had shown that countries were willing to cooperate but needed to be prodded by a more solid framework for reaction.

Canada prompted more than 20 countries including France, Britain, Belgium, Senegal and South Africa to promise to contribute to a 10,000-strong Canadian-led force intended to rescue more than one million refugees stranded in Zaire.

After hundreds of thousands of refugees began flooding back across the border into Rwanda, however, the mission had to be rethought and now includes plans for an aid airdrop, backed up by between 1,000 and 2,000 troops.
He said the way this disaster had unfolded showed how vital it was to harmonise the way governments, the military, non-governmental organisations and humanitarian aid agencies approached such crises.
Chretien said it was up to security bodies to develop a plan to deal with such disasters as the very definition of security had changed.
"Human conflict is our greatest enemy and constitutes the greatest enemy to the values we stand for," he said.
"Today the image is not of armies of soldiers but armies of displaced people and refugeees, of the hungry, the sick and the stateless," he added.
Chretien told the summit, which groups the United States and Canada with all European states, that the world community had looked on as predictable crises such as Zaire had developed.

"Better mechanisms of conflict prevention and a stronger will on the part of the international community to intervene in an area where few national interests were at stake might well have headed of these disasters," he said.
Although the OSCE is not empowered to operate outside its geographic limits, Chretien said it could draw lessons from Zaire and other cases such as Somalia, northern Iraq and former Yugoslavia.
"We should dedicate ourselves to find better ways of ensuring that ad hoc solutions do not have to be relied upon in the future," he said.
